newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile to vote on bill to legalize divorce.
newsitem.headline: Chile to vote on bill to legalize divorce.

text.p: Chilean legislators were expected to vote early on Friday on a controversial bill that would legalise divorce in the Catholic country.

Chile, known for its conservative social mores, is among only a handful of nations that do not allow divorce. In a fiery debate in Congress on Thursday, supporters said the bill would give a second chance to people in failed marriages and give the children of separated parents the full legal status of those born in wedlock.

"Children born out of matrimony in some cases are not allowed to matriculate in school. Is that being a good Catholic?" asked supporter Ivan Moreira of the right-wing Democratic Independent Union (UDI).

The bill has cut sharply across party lines, with some members of rightist parties supporting but most opposing it. President Eduardo Frei's Christian Demcratic Party is also divided, although Frei himself is believed to back the bill.
If the Chamber of Deputies passes the bill, it will still face strong opposition in the Senate, where rightists and military-appointed senators hold a majority.

With no divorce, Chilean couples frequently live out of wedlock or obtain an annulment of their marriage. The children of such unions live in a kind of legal limbo without the full rights or social standing of others.
Opponents of the divorce law said it will break down the family structure and act as an incitement for troubled marriages to split up rather than reconcile.

Argentina enacted a divorce law in 1987 and voters in Ireland narrowly approved a divorce law in a referendum in 1995, leaving conservative Chile as of one of the very few countries in the world with no divorce.
Opposition from the Roman Catholic Church has so far been muted, although bishops have criticised the bill in sermons.
